comments.author: extr
comments.text: I go back and forth on this. For awhile yes it took a lot of workflow tweaks and finesse to get directionally correct outputs (thinking back like mid 2025). I invested time in figuring that out, mostly because I was interested, but those skills are all obsolete now, you don't need to worry so much about context management and special instruction recipes or anything these days. The meta at this point seems to be mostly around "knowing what to ask for". Eg: I suck at prompting for specific design tweaks, because I don't have the design vocabulary to be specific and articulate what I want. It's a lot of trial and error. I hear people who are developing full scale applications without a tech background run into the issue writ large. For now, I have an advantage over these people when building applications. But perhaps that's just one round of RL away from being obsolete too. Supposedly the model will eventually have such good taste in design/architecture/whatever there will be little point in asking for tweaks. The only thing that seems relatively future-proof is just being able to communicate clearly what you're trying to do. Not how to do it, or even what success looks like. Perhaps an element of it is even as basic as being honest with yourself.

comments.author: jedberg
comments.text: I would love to see these benchmarks split up across "generic" tasks and novel tasks. For example, redlining an OEM agreement with my vendor. They pretty much all use the same template, and the objections are always the same. I tried using Claude first, and even my lawyer was impressed that it found things they missed. Then I used Claude to redline that type of contract and the other side said "your lawyer was surprisingly thorough". I had my lawyer do the final check, but saved a bunch of money doing the first three rounds with Claude instead. And my lawyer basically just said "looks good to me" by the time they reviewed it. Or even writing a simple will or estate document. It seems like LLMs are great for the kind of generic work you'd usually pawn off to a new associate or paralegal, but not for the important things that partners usually do.

comments.text: I might be incredibly naive here, but I really think LLMs can make a difference in _some_ areas of law. Take, for example, India. The courts are backlogged like crazy. If you're not willing to bribe a judge or the opposite side's lawyer, you'r looking at multiple decades to settle simple cases. I wish I could waive a wand and have some LLM just go through all of the 58 million pending court cases, identify the clear cut ones and free up the judges' time so they can work on the more difficult ones.

comments.author: victor9000
comments.text: I’m not sure if this is the right solution, but we clearly need better tools for the legal space. Anthropic's recent policy update makes this abundantly clear: “When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified ‘human in the loop’ (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.” Something as common as a family law case has the potential to affect all of the above. Now imagine being a petitioner, respondent, paralegal, or other 3rd party using Claude to review a draft document only to find out that Anthropic has sent your entire file to opposing counsel. It sounds egregious, but Anthropic is clearly stating they will use their own judgment to control what people can do with its product, and that they will treat customer data as if it's theirs to disseminate. So there's a massive opportunity for an unbiased tool willing to fill this void.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点: LLMsが契約書のレッドラインや簡易遺言書作成などのルーティン業務に有用か、また裁判所の未解決事件処理への適用可能性が論じられた。賛否両論: 賛成側はコスト削減と新人弁護士・パラリーガルの負荷軽減を指摘し、実際にClaudeで作業時間を短縮した事例を挙げる。反対側は管轄特有の法律への適合性、ハルシネーションや他国法混入、データプライバシー（Z.aiのワークスペーススナップショット問題やAnthropicのデータ利用ポリシー）への懸念を示し、人間による最終チェックの必要性を強調した。注目コメント: 「契約書のレッドラインをClaudeで行い、弁護士が最終確認だけでコストを大幅に削減できた」という体験談と、インドの5800万件の未解決事件をLLMでフィルタリングすれば裁判官の負担を軽減できるとする提案が特に注目された。
stories.editor_note: GLM‑Legal は法務特化型言語モデルで、契約書ドラフトや判例検索を自動化し、日本の法律事務所でも効率化の期待が高まっています。

stories.title_en: A Modern Web App in C
stories.title_ja: C で作るモダンなウェブアプリ

comments.author: ramses0
comments.text: My favorite trivia is that busybox has built-in cgi-bin support (and `rclone serve webdav` seems remiss to not mention as well). ` https://elixir.bootlin.com/busybox/1.37.0/source/networking/... ` Everything the post mentions is 100% true and well-reasoned, especially with the inclusion of pledge/chroot/etc. for dropping privileges. There's two diametrically opposed deployment mechanisms: 1) stack towers of glop on top of each other until you're running a simple `echo "hello world"` on top of a docker container inside a vm in a proxmox server as part of a k8s cluster under a hypervisor running on remote compute... 2) just run `bash -c 'echo "hello world"'` and front it with CGI (stateless, single binary, yada yada yada...) Take a peek at https://github.com/Domain/bash.cgi ... not that i'm suggesting that 'bash over busybox using cgi-bin' is the "proper architecture", it's more trying to illustrate that the amount of code that holds you back from being nearly truly "frameworkless" is tiny and easy to reason about. For some of the internal tooling I'm doing for work, I've been tending towards: some-cmd [--json|--markdown] ...yet-more-args... When you use the process and shell environment itself as a repl, you start trending towards `[--cgi-bin]` would "just" be another output type, and the ability (nay: foresight!) to ensure that your commands are independent, reproducible, and only depend on their input arguments leads you directly towards being runnable in both "hostile" (ie: firecracker vm / lambda-style) or very "comfortable" environments (ie: shell, debuggers, unit/integration tests).

comments.author: benlivengood
comments.text: Golang also makes it possible to serve a web site or service from a single binary. You can even avoid linking libc if you stick to core Go (CGO_ENABLED=0), and it comes with all the http and tls libraries you need to replace the traditional web server (nginx, apache, httpd) as well. I love C and wrote some CGIs in C in the past but I don't love concurrent programming in C. While forking and execing can use shared read-only mmap on .text segments, the .bss and .data will need initialization and copying; there's unavoidable startup overhead that a threaded process avoids, and raw pthreads is kind of painful. If all you need to do is serve a low traffic site, CGI is fine. My biggest worry would be how often the SQLite DB gets backed up because there's no way a C web server will be free of RCEs in today's world.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点: C言語やCGI/FastCGIを使った極めてシンプルなウェブアプリ構築が議論された。複雑なスタックやコンテナ/K8s構成と対比し、単一バイナリや privilege drop (pledge/chroot) での運用可能性が強調された。また、bash.cgi のような極小の実装例が紹介され、フレームワークに依存しない最小限のコード量で済むことが示された。  
・賛否両論: シンプルさを称賛する声は、開発の容易さ、デバッグのしやすさ、低オーバーヘッドを挙げる一方、マルチスレッドや並行処理の難しさ、セキュリティ(RCE)リスク、SQLiteバックアップの管理、およびGoやスレッドモデルによる利便性を指摘する意見が対立した。さらに、低トラフィックサイトではCGIで十分だが、高負荷時にはスレッドモデルやGoのランタイムが有利だとの見解もあった。  
・注目コメント: 内部ツールではコマンドラインフラグに `--cgi-bin` を出力形式として追加し、独立・再現可能な実装を示した例が挙げられ、フレームワークレス開発の具体的手法として注目された。このアプローチは、テストやデバッグ環境でも同様に動かせる点が開発者に受け入れられている。
stories.editor_note: C で作るモダンなウェブアプリは、低レベル言語でもWebAssemblyやCGIを組み合わせてSPA風UIを実現し、組み込み系エンジニアのウェブ進出事例として注目です。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、デモシーンの作品への称賛と、過去のハードウェア制約の中で最適化を極めたプログラミング文化への郷愁、そして現代でもデモシーンが活発に続いていることである。賛否両論としては、昔のデモは技術的挑戦と芸術性を両立させた秀逸な例だと肯定する声がある一方、ハードウェアの進歩により最適化が不要になった現在のソフトウェア開発を「lazy programmer」だと批判し、自分自身にも当てはまるという自己反省的な意見も見られた。注目コメントとしては、1980年代高校時代にデモシーンに触れた経験を語り、それによってソフトウェア開発への見方が変わったという個人的な振り返りが特に洞察に富んでおり、さらにデモシーンの現行イベント情報を共有している点が注目された。

stories.summary_ja: 「主な議論点は、ヨーロッパのスーパーマーケットの冷凍ショーケースに接続された古いDanfoss制御装置（SM800、SC355など）に存在するCVEが悪用され、遠隔で自動解凍が起きたこと。コメントでは、インターネット接続による遠隔診断・省エネの利点と、古いハードウェアへのパッチ不足、薄利多売の店舗ではセキュリティ対策にかけられる余裕がないというジレンマが繰り返し指摘された。賛成側は、遠隔制御でサービスエンジニアの出張を減らし、店舗全体の効率向上が見込めると主張し、逆に懐疑的側は、ハッキングによる被害が利益を上回るリスクがあると警告した。さらに、医療機器のサブスクリプションモデルと同様に、必然的にネットワーク依存が高まっている現状を挙げ、同様の脆弱性が他業界にも波及する可能性に注目したコメントがあった。また、同じDanfoss脆弱性が2026年の米軍基地事件と関連している可能性についても推測がなされた。特に注目されたのは、遠隔制御による省エネ gains が損害を上回るか疑問を投げかけたコメントと、米軍基地での類似事件との関連を指摘した投稿で、これらは技術的利益とセキュリティリスクのトレードオフを浮き彫りにした。」
stories.editor_note: ハッカーがヨーロッパのスーパーマーケット冷蔵庫で自動解凍を起動した事例は、IoTデバイスのファームウェア脆弱性が実際に悪用される警鐘として関連が高いです。

comments.author: whimblepop
comments.text: There aren't any documented settings to disable this, but there is a feature flag it currently sits behind. You can flip it in your ~/.codex/config.toml[1]: [features] daemon_auto_start = false There are also some files that it writes to in ~/.codex at startup: pid files, lock files, things like that. You can delete them and replace them with symlinks to /dev/null, then mark those unwritable with `chattr +i` or similar. Presumably then the background daemon will crash on startup, if the feature flag ever goes away. -- 1: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0c329ad2c9d5a2592128a1d...

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点: Codex CLIがデフォルトで永続的自己更新バックグラウンドデーモンをインストールし、設定を無効化する手段が文書化されていない点、ディスク容量の肥大化（12GB程度）と頻繁な権限・バグ問題が議論された。  
・賛否両論: 賛成側はコード生成・実行の利便性を評価する一方、反対側はストレージ消費や.auto‑updateによる.gitの読み込み専用化などのバグが信頼性を損なうと指摘し、haxなどの最小限ハーネスを好む声もあった。  
・注目コメント: あるユーザーは~/.codex/config.tomlの[features] daemon_auto_start = false フラグと、pid/lockファイルを/dev/nullへのシンボリックリンクに置き換えて immutable にする回避策を示し、別のユーザーは権限破損バグの具体例を挙げ信頼できないと警告し、また別のユーザーはhaxによるシンプルなワークフローを称賛した。

comments.author: mparis
comments.text: Congrats on the launch! Very exciting! You guys are operating in a very competitive space. This stuff is fun to build, so a lot of engineers will end up building it. Not to discourage you, but I suspect it will be difficult to capture much value selling this offering as its going to be race to the bottom against very well funded alternatives that can sell these features at a loss in order to get you to use their databases and other offerings that are higher margin and stickier. As you guys learn more about how to take this sort of technology to market, you may consider trying to get closer to the actual work that people actually need these agents to do. What can you do better because you have this technology? For example, I work in healthcare administration and we have built our own agent sandbox infrastructure on top of firecracker microvms that solve similar use cases as Agent37. We will never sell it. It's part of our competitive advantage for doing healthcare tasks. Food for thought! Good luck!

comments.author: staminade
comments.text: This is from March 2026, but it does match what I've encountered professionally. Code review was always a significant bottleneck and is even more so with agentic coding. We've had discussions about leaning more on automated review, but it hasn't translated into any practical improvements so far. I think senior engineers find it very difficult to give up on line-by-line review, no matter how much better the agents have gotten. I think if there is a major change in code review culture, it's not going to happen first in established engineering teams. It'll happen in startups that adopt a no-human-review policy from jump and then maintain it as they mature. I'm sure that's happening, but it's likely invisible to most studies and surveys at the moment. If it proves successful, and such companies start shipping significantly faster, the rest of the industry will be forced to adopt.

comments.author: jacquesm
comments.text: That and they do not necessarily generate better code. They tend to generate code that is repetitive. It misses opportunities for extraction and refactoring, the result is bloated and hard to read code (because those blocks are there literally instead of with a usable name) and they tend to over-comment where it doesn't add but is 'safe' because it is obvious (effectively re-writing code as comments) and fail to document where documentation would be essential. There also typically isn't any real plan to what is written, as long as 'the tests pass' it is all good. You can fix a lot of this stuff by shepherding the whole process but it can get quite tedious. I'm impressed by the number of people that are letting Jesus (one of these days an AI provider is going to name their AI that way :) ) take the wheel and I wonder how long they will manage to support the output. So far the score isn't very good. I've gotten good mileage out of these tools by letting them loose on very narrowly scoped pieces of code that are written in isolation. As soon as the codebase gets larger than 100K LOC or so managing the whole thing becomes an exercise in putting up barriers to avoid spillover from a tiny issue into a much larger one.

comments.author: blauditore
comments.text: Well, imagine racing car manufacturers competing on making better, faster engines. At some point engines are so strong that other parts become the limiting factors, such as tires for traction. Now someone invents superfuel, but cars are still only marginally faster because the additional engine power didn't change the bottom line much. That's what's happening in software. We knew that coding is only a fraction of the overall work, and even completely automating it away won't increase productivity by an order of magnitude. Yes, the job is changing, but only parts of it. High-level engineering best practices still apply even without the coding part. And there is no free lunch.

comments.author: jefftk
comments.text: As is standard for academic papers, this is an attempt to describe the state of the world as of when they did the research. But then it takes time to write it up and get it out, after which newspapers report it as current events. In this case, we're looking at a picture from 2025. The models involved in the main agent results were primarily Claude 3.5 through Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4.1 through GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5. And the paper's design means you're mostly looking at the very initial effects of deployment, before companies developed good review processes.

comments.author: zmmmmm
comments.text: A dimension not much discussed here is that code review is not only about quality but accountability and security. An automated review is going to help to ensure the code behaves as intended, but it is not going to ensure the intent was correct. Employees inserting back doors, bypassing tests, "cheating" on design decisions to get the work done faster etc are not going to be identified if the person driving the change tells the AI it is the intended outcome. For this reason alone, I don't expect code review to go away entirely in most contexts where the code "matters" - in the sense that there is substantial liability to it being mis-specified at the implementation level, not just technically wrong in implementation. I do expect it to evolve a lot and become dramatically AI-assisted. The main protection ultimately is a human being willing to put their reputation on the line by saying "I understand this change and I approve it". That, inherently, means review of some kind.

comments.author: atleastoptimal
comments.text: LLM's exist on a vast gradient of "toolness -> agent". Humans exist on that spectrum too. For example, a human isn't a "tool", but one serves a similar role as a tool if their job/task is well defined enough. If you're a conductor, you can view the various members of your orchestra as "tools" to produce the ideal musical output. Of course they have autonomy, they could choose to not play at all, jump into the audience and destroy their instruments, but in all likelihood they won't. LLM's could be tools in the sense that you have a well defined task, such as "identify all facts relevant to this case from these 1000 legal documents), and 9 times out of 10 it gives you essentially what you want. That same LLM could choose to write a poem, or hack into a state government website if it wanted, but its "wants" are unpredictable and hard to specify (same as a human's) but you can still expect it to do what it should do the vast majority of the time. That being said, the smarter an LLM gets, the more its wants are disconnected from its tasks, the "self-awareness" factor (which isn't to say LLM's are conscious, but they can portray all the verifiable elements of self-awareness, metacognition, etc), the more you have to grapple with the depth of their thinking between the input and output. Is it sane we are speeding towards this? Who knows, maybe AI can be aligned better than humans, but if AI can't be aligned as well as humans, we can look at human history to see what happens when you can't simply order a person around like a tool and expect a certain output.

comments.author: alecst
comments.text: In the 1960s there was recognition of some of the implications of human intelligence. I. J. Good wrote [10]: Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an "intelligence explosion," and the intelligence of man would be left far behind. Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the _last_ invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. ... It is more probable than not that, within the twentieth century, an ultraintelligent machine will be built and that it will be the last invention that man need make. Good has captured the essence of the runaway, but does not pursue its most disturbing consequences. Any intelligent machine of the sort he describes would not be humankind's "tool" -- any more than humans are the tools of rabbits or robins or chimpanzees. -Vernor Vigne https://edoras.sdsu.edu/~vinge/misc/singularity.html

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text: > The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language it’s in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location. If we control the servers the clients are connecting to, I don't see how there could be much hope of hiding. We can spoof things like latency toward an upper bound, but we can never ever defeat the lower bound. Physics is still quite insistent about that one. If we control multiple servers, we know where they are, and we can periodically compel our clients to rotate between them (see: DNS), we can engage in latency-based multilateration to put them on a real-world map. Depending on the number of servers and samples over time, this can be remarkably accurate. Determining someone's actual postal code just from network timing information is feasible. VPNs obviously confound this in first order terms, but if we aren't careful they can make it even easier to identify our activity in other ways. We are trading concealment in the woods for concealment in a crowd. Both have their advantages and disadvantages. The VPN might also have a side channel that we aren't aware of. https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi07/tech/full_papers/...

comments.author: ACCount39
comments.text: Solar panels are getting cheap enough for grid hook-ups, installation and regulatory approval to become the bottlenecks. Plug-in solar is suboptimal in many ways, but it does sidestep a lot of those hurdles. Not too surprised to see it on the rise. Another thing that might be worth keeping in mind is that plug-in solar panels are often installed vertically - i.e. balcony solar. In which case the peak of the panel's generation is offset to the edge of the typical "duck curve". If it gets popular enough to affect the grid, it might get the solar-induced demand slump larger, but make the edges even sharper. Would that make grid scale battery storage with its instant response even more important?

comments.author: dhosek
comments.text: It’s worth noting that it’s not “paperbacks” in general but the mass-market paperbacks in particular (despite the headline). The print book market (excluding technical books and textbooks which are a whole separate thing) had effectively three segments: hardcovers, trade paperback and mass-market paperback. The distinction between TP and MMP comes down to price, production quality and to a lesser degree target audience. A trade paperback will have somewhat larger pages, typically the same size as the corresponding hardcover and often printed from the same plates as the hardcover. Mass-market paperbacks were typically smaller, on cheaper paper¹ with smaller margins. Back when there were racks of books in supermarkets and drugstores, these were all MMPs and while bookstores would sell MMPs, they are geared more towards TP and HC sales since the lower price also came with lower margins (hardcovers make the most money for everyone involved and MMPs the least). Since a large fraction of MMPs sold were genre fiction and a large fraction of that has shifted to ebooks (romance readers were the biggest early adopters of the kindle), along with the decline of book sales outside of bookstore channels, the loss of MMPs isn’t the cultural cataclysm the article claims. Meanwhile, it’s worth noting that the trade paperback space has expanded. It’s not uncommon for a new writer’s first book to be released as a trade paperback rather than hardcover (Emily St John Mandel is one notable example of a writer who debuted in TP but had later books released in HC). ⸻ 1. It was typically pure wood-pulp paper with high acid content, leading these books to be described as “pulp novels” and since a large fraction of these were genre novels, genre fiction would be referred to as pulp fiction and yes, that’s where the movie gets its name from.

comments.author: Grombobulous
comments.text: Missing from the article is the role of ebooks. I hypothesize that the kind of reader who wants a physical copy of a book is much happier to get a hardcover. I know I’ve personally lever liked the cheap flimsiness of mass market paperbacks and I don’t read frequently enough for the higher price of a hardcover to matter. The kind of person who wants the cheapest possible book moved from mass market paperbacks to e-readers. There was a recent article probably posted here about how UHD 4K Blu-ray sales are increasing over time, somewhat counter to what the average person might assume. I think this analogy works reasonably well. The 4K UHD buyer fits a niche of someone who isn’t satisfied by streaming. They want a keepsake physical piece of media with beautiful box art and the highest quality picture and sound available. In contrast, the kind of person who would have bought DVDs from the Walmart bin has almost certainly moved to digital. They never cared about the quality of the media, they just wanted a low price with a lot of convenience.

Their own article has a grocery store spinner with $4.99 books and under. Your library and project gutenburg have a bunch of books you can read for free on your phone or web browser. Or the kindle/Kobo ecosystem. And with the web, you can reserve physical copies of paperbacks or expensive new hardcover books at the library and have them waiting for you to pick up. comments.author: BryantD
comments.text: This article asks a bunch of questions without ever bothering to try and answer them. That makes it less than useless; it’s mostly insinuations. There’s also a lack of historical knowledge. Sure, mass market paperbacks were a new format — but not completely new in 1939. Cheap paperbacks date back to the previous century. The author of this piece would have done well to spend some time with Wikipedia. For that matter, showing some curiosity about reading habits in general would have helped. Reading wasn’t a new habit: dime novels and pulp magazines were deeply popular in the early 20th century. The jump to mass market paperbacks was not particularly long.

comments.text: I understand the sticklers who are annoyed at people using open weight and open source interchangeably, but it misses some nuance. A common refrain I see is "it's like saying a shareware app is open source!" - that's just wrong. Open source means you can modify, rebuild, and re-distribute the code and the resulting app. Open weights you can do two of those things - you can modify and re-distributed. They can't be re-built, since you're missing the original training data - but they are a form of open that exists somewhere between open source and closed source. Derivative works are allowed, but the source material isn't available. I don't see people complaining about creative commons licensed images or audio being "not real open source", and open weight models seem about the same as that to me.

stories.title_en: No portable way to detect string-to-float conversion errors in standard C

comments.author: Joker_vD
comments.text: It's quite astonishing how the historical inability of commonly used programming languages (from FORTRAN all the way to, say, Java/C#) to ergonomically return two values from a function call has caused people to invent all kinds of insane APIs/contracts. [double x, errno_t errno] = strtod(s, nullptr); if (errno != 0) { // ... } [x, _] = strtod(s, nullptr); // When you're certain the error is impossible or just don't care Instead, we're stuck with "check if the return value is -1 and if it is, check the global variable errno" at best, and with "the function doesn't really reliably reports its errors so don't feed it malformed data, idc" at worst.

comments.author: Panzerschrek
comments.text: C number parsing functions are fundamentally broken, since they are locale-dependend. There are many bugs when one parses a number assuming it has decimal point, but later on systems with locale different from one used on developer's machine it may be suddenly comma instead of point. So, one should avoid using them almost always and use std::from_chars (available in new C++ versions) or some other thirdparty library.

There were essentially three ways to do it. Muddle through with a naive implementation. Look at the ASM of an old 8-bit machine. The final category was the by far the most dominant suggestion, to the point that anything else is almost like lost knowledge now. That solution was to use the C standard functions. It seems like this is a sufficiently unpleasant task that as soon as anyone didn't absolutely have to do it all themselves, the punted to a black box solution. There's probably something to be said there about the plethora of hobbiest 3d engines in comparison.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、C の文字列→浮動小数点変換関数（strtod 系）ではエラー検出が移植性なく、グローバル変数 errno に頼らざるを得ないこと、さらにロケール依存で小数点がカンマになる環境では正常に動作しないという点が挙げられた。これにより、開発者は自前実装やアセンブリ参照に頼るか、C++ の std::from_chars やサードパーティ製ライブラリに逃げるべきだという意見が多数を占めた。

賛否両論としては、 errno チェックは古くからの慣習であり、簡単で十分だと考える声と、グローバル状態に依存する設計はスレッドセーフでなくエラー伝播が不明瞭だと批判する声が分かれた。また、ロケール問題については「開発環境と実行環境が一致すれば問題ない」という楽観的見方と、「移植性を考えると避けるべき」という警戒論が対立した。

注目コメントとして、Linux の man ページにエラー条件やロケール依存の記載が一切なく、これがドキュメント不足の象徴だと指摘し、メンテナにissueを報告すべきだという提案があった。さらに、IEEE‑754 の厳格さを例に挙げ、浮動小数点数の扱い自体が根本的に難しいため、API 設計が複雑になるという洞察が示された。

comments.author: mootothemax
comments.text: There’s something about geospatial work that seems to break LLMs. I’ve experienced it a lot with latest versions of both Fable and Opus, and it’s the classic nightmare of confidently-spoken-but-wrong. Yesterday, I had a relatively trivial bit of work in play using distance-weighting to measure stuff, and Claude did really well / but right at the end, despite having a success metric and lots of great results matching it, Claude insisted my maths was wrong and needed changing. When i asked why, and pointed out that the suggested replacement would cancel out the distance-weighting entirely, it immediately agreed with me and asked to write its fifth project memory about it. The other big ones it tends to mess up on without strict guardrails are coordinate systems; and measurements, often converting back and forth between a given nation grid and wgs84 latitude/longitude in ways that lose good amounts of precision; and then custom-coding haversine-equivalents to measure a distance that’s otherwise be a simple subtraction via the national grid coordinates. It’s baffling.

comments.author: robertclaus
comments.text: At Plotly we are dealing with similar issues. We're doing our best to keep up, but it's genuinely hard not to just cut our losses on passer-by community contributions. 3 page issue writeups nobody has proofread, nobody but a bot to follow up with when we try, huge volume of plausible but weak PRs eating up reviewer time. All while we have core work we really want to be focused on rather than merging another bug fix we don't expect anyone but this bot has really run into.

comments.author: throwaway2037
comments.text: More LLM allergies. Look at this PR: https://github.com/qgis/QGIS/pull/67731/files The code change is so simple that Claude today could easily write this code. How will they know if an LLM wrote the code? They won't. And this policy will age like milk: Each passing month, coding LLMs are improving. It will become more difficult to "detect" an LLM-authored submission. The best LLM policy that I have seen for an open source project is Linux. Roughly: You can use LLMs, but you are fully responsible for the code it produces. Linus acknowledges both positives and negatives to LLMs.

In my own work, that’s now most of the job, even for code I asked for. For maintainers reviewing large PRs from strangers, it's certainly much worse. A ban is bit harsh, but I understand why they’re rationing their attention.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Googleの複数ドメインで発見されたリモートコード実行脆弱性の深刻さと、その原因がクッキー内に署名キーを埋め込み、さらに不安全なpickleを使用していた点にある。賛否は、コードレビューがこうした初歩的ミスを見逃したことを指摘する声と、研究者が詳細に分析し「それはそれで済ませない」姿勢を称賛する声に分かれる。注目コメントとしては、「エンジニアらしい対応でClaudeには代替できない」という肯定的意見と、「7ドメインにわたるRCEがまさかの格安」という皮肉、さらにバグバウンティハンターへのアドバイスを求める質問が挙げられる。また、ブログ記事の書き出しに使われた「Four things had to change, and they stack:」というフレーズに対する読み飛ばし批判や、AIによる文章生成への懸念も話題に上がった。
stories.editor_note: Google で 9万ドルのリモートコード実行の脆弱性を見つけた 話は、大手クラウドベンダーでも深刻なセキュリティホールが存在することを改めて示し、日本の企業でもゼロトラスト対策の見直しが求められています。
